On Becoming a Physician: Perspectives of Students in Combined Baccalaureate-MD Degree Programs Lynn C. Epstein Brown University Jeannie Hayes and Louise Arnold University of Missouri-Kansas City Patricia O'SulIivan Baystate Medical Center Alexis L. Ruffin and Larry Rogers Association of American Medical Colleges Bonnie Jones Northeastern Ohio Universities Selma Van Eyck University of Wisconsin Donald Brown University of Michigan Robert Hinkley University of Miami Harry Linde Northwestern University Paul O'Bryan Boston University Willard Roth Union College Students entering the first year of nine combined baccalaureate-MD degree (CD) programs were administered the Matriculating Student Questionnaire (MSQ) of the Association of American Medical Colleges. A profile of the CD students' perspectives on becoming a physician was compared with the profile oftraditional medical students who responded to the MSQ. CD students chose medicine as a career goal earlier in life than their traditional counterparts. They also had more positive perceptions of medicine. Their decisions regarding future career interests in medicine differed in some respects from those of traditional students. Larger percentages of CD students were female, had Asian backgrounds, and had physician fathers. The views of CD students were partly related to the type of CD program they attended and to demo- graphic/background characteristics, including age, which was suggested by prelimi- nary comparisons between premedical students and CD students. It was recently reported that students entering a medical school with an innovative admissions process and a curriculum stressing a biopsychosocial approach to health care differed significantly from peers matric- ulating to two traditional schools.1 Do other innovative schools also recruit different types of students? Indeed, with respect to family background, career decisions, and perceptions of medicine, freshmen entering a com- bined baccalaureate-MD degree program (CD) at Brown University directly after high school graduation have been found to differ from students beginning medical school after college.2 It may be that students entering other CD programs also differ from students following more traditional paths to the MD degree. Examining this possibility can increase our insight into how students entering innovative and traditional schools compare and contrast. That insight is a first step to understanding the antecedents to educational out- comes of innovative and traditional approaches to med- ical education. Nine CD programs collaborated with staff at the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) to generate a profile of their entering CD students, to ascertain how that profile compared with a national profile of students undertaking their medical educa- tion after college graduation, and to explore some of the bases for differences between profiles of CD and traditional students. The profile highlights key issues related to students' decisions to become physi- cians—when and why they selected a career in med- icine and how they envision their own future as physicians. Method In the fall of 1990, nine CD schools (see Table 1) surveyed their entering students by administering the AAMC Matriculating Student Questionnaire (MSQ). The MSQ consists of 50 questions about respondents' demographic characteristics, perceptions of medicine, and career plans and interests. It is typically given to first-year students entering medical school after college graduation. We made minor modifications to the MSQ to achieve appropriate wording for administration to CD students. Each CD school listed in the 1990-1991 edition of the AAMC Medical School Admission Require- ments3 was invited to collaborate in this study. The nine CD schools that elected to participate represent established schools with large student bodies; their combined enrollment accounts for more than one half of all CD students. The response rates for the nine CD schools ranged from 83% to 100% (Table 1) and yielded a sample of 481 CD respondents for this study. Single sample tests of proportions were used to de- termine if the responses of the CD sample to selected MSQ items were representative of the population of traditional students typically entering medical school after 4 years of college. The database for the national population was collected by the AAMC in the fall of 1990. The level of significance for these analyses was set at .001 for an overall Type I error rate of .10 for the number of tests made. On other MSQ items, two-tailed t tests were used to detect differences between mean responses of CD and traditional students; the signifi- cance level was again set at .001. The conservative significance level is particularly appropriate for testing the underlying hypothesis that there would be differ- ences between the CD and traditional students' per- spectives on becoming a physician. One explana- tion for obtained differences was sought among the types of programs CD students attended. Accordingly, when the responses of CD and traditional students to MSQ items differed significantly, chi-square analyses were performed to ascertain if the CD students' an- swers to those questions were associated with the cur- ricular length of their program (6,7, or 8 years) and with the public or private control of their school. A second explanation for contrasting responses of CD and tradi- tional students was sought among the demographic and background characteristics that distinguished the CD students from their traditional counterparts. As Table 2 indicates, CD students were much more likely to be female, to have Asian backgrounds, and to have physi- cian fathers. Thus, when the answers of CD and tradi- tional students to MSQ items differed, chi-square analyses were run to determine whether the responses of CD students on these items were related to these three background characteristics. In addition, the age of CD and traditional students differed; on average, CD students were 18 years old, traditional students 24 years old. Thus, another explanation for different responses by the CD and traditional students was sought in the age differential between these students. Age of premedical stu- dents averaged 18 years; their ethnic backgrounds and the occupations of their fathers, however, resembled more closely those of the traditional rather than those of the CD students (Table 2). The responses of the premedical students were included to provide prelimi- nary information. For the chi-square analyses, the level of significance was set at .05 to accommodate the exploratory nature of this part of the study. No statistical analyses were used to examine the premedical students' responses in relation to CD or traditional students because of the size and the convenience nature of the premedical student sample. Rather, descriptive statistics are reported. Results Although similar in some respects, the perspectives CD and traditional students held about medicine dif- fered in important ways. Deciding to Be a Physician When. Virtually all CD students (97%) but only half the traditional students (52%) decided before high school graduation that they definitely wanted to be physicians. In fact, a third of the CD students (35%) knew before they began high school that they definitely wanted to be physicians, whereas only one fourth of the traditional students had reached a firm decision by then. More CD students in 6-year programs (43%) and 7-year programs (38%) as opposed to those in 8-year programs (16%) made a definite decision to study medicine before high school, %2(4, N = 479) = 25.2, p - .001. The gender, ethnic background, and occupation of fathers of CD students were not associated with the timing of their decision to become physicians. Forty- five percent of the premedical students, however, said they knew before entering high school that they defi- nitely wanted to study medicine. Why. Both CD and traditional students cited their interest in helping people, the intellectual challenge of medicine, and the opportunity to use special talents and abilities as the top factors in their choice of medicine for their careers (see Table 3). In making this decision, however, CD students found the intellectual challenge of medicine less important than did traditional students (Table 3). Yet, compared to traditional students, CD students thought the opportunity for research in medi- cine a more important consideration in their career choice (Table 3). In addition, compared to traditional students, CD students assigned greater importance to job security, income, and prestige in their career choice and attributed more importance to the encouragement of other people in their decision (Table 3). The length of the CD program and the ethnic back- ground of CD students were associated with several of these differences between CD and traditional students' reasons for deciding to study medicine. Specifically, more CD students in 6-year programs said job security, income, and prestige were very important factors in their choice of medicine than did students from 7- and 8-year programs—for job security, 6-year students = 45%, 7-year students = 31%, 8-year students = 27%, %2(6, N = 475) = 26.0, p = .001; for income, 6-year students = 25%, 7-year students = 14%, 8-year students = 13%, X2(8, N = 479) = 16.7, p = .03; for prestige, 6-year students = 23%, 7-year students = 15%, 8-year students = 12%, x2(8, W=476) = 20.8, p = .008. Fewer of the CD students with physi- cian fathers thought the intellectual challenge of med- icine was important in their choice of medicine than did CD students whose fathers were in other occupations and professions—students with physician fathers = 42%, students with nonphysician fathers = 58%, %2(3, N = 476) = 8.8, p = .03. The importance premedical students gave to factors in their decision to study med- icine typically paralleled the importance assigned to the factors by CD students (Table 3). The parallel is partic- ularly striking with regard to the emphasis CD and premedical students gave to job security, income, pres- tige, and research interests. However, premedical stu- dents rated the encouragement of others as less important in their decision to study medicine than did CD students (Table 3). Perceptions. CD and traditional students both rec- ognized the same benefits to being a physician (Table 4). A majority of both types of students agreed that advances in the medical sciences and their application to patient care will make medicine more stimulating, challenging, and fulfilling in the future; that having interesting and intelligent colleagues would be a major benefit of being a physician; and that opportunities to build a successful practice are always available to phy- sicians who work hard. Yet, CD and traditional students held contrasting perceptions of the disadvantages to medical practice in the future. Compared to traditional students, fewer CD students believed that changes in the health care system will impair physicians' independence, that medicine will not be as financially rewarding in the future as it is today, and that physicians will not receive the same respect (Table 4). Further, CD students were less likely to say that a medical career would interfere with family relations or other interests (Table 4). In these respects, CD students were more optimistic about medicine than traditional students were. The curricular length of the CD programs was related to their students' perception of the financial rewards of medicine in the future—a point of disagreement be- tween CD and traditional students. More specifically, students in 6- and 7-year programs were less likely to agree that medicine will not be as financially rewarding than were CD students in 8-year programs—6-year students = 54%, 7-year students=58%, 8-year students = 70%, %\4, N = 480) = 15.3, p = .004. CD students' gender, ethnicity, and fathers' occupations were not associated with the differences between the CD and traditional students' perceptions of medicine's disad- vantages. However, compared to CD students, premed- ical students were even more sanguine about the disadvantages to medicine, save one (Table 4). Future Career Patterns Major activities. But CD students (88%) were significantly more likely to be interested in clinical practice than were traditional students (81%), whereas traditional students (15%) planned on full-time academic service more often than CD students (5%.) More students in 6- and 7-year programs were inclined toward clinical practice than those in 8-year programs—6-year stu- dents = 91%, 7-year students = 90%, 8-year students = 76%, %2(2, N = 474) = 13.5, p = .001. CD students' gender, ethnicity, and fathers' occupations were not related to the differences in career activities preferred by CD and traditional students. Among the premedical students, 86% were interested in clinical practice, and 6% were interested in academic medicine. Specialty. Most typically, both CD students (86%) and traditional students (86%) were undecided about their future specialty choice. A majority of both the CD students (58%) and the traditional students (61%) hoped to seek certification in a specialty but did not know which specialty they would pursue. Similarly, almost one fourth of both the CD students (28%) and the traditional students (25%) were not sure they would specialize, although very few CD and traditional stu- dents endorsed the perception that specialists were less important than primary care doctors (Table 4). Practice location and the underserved. CD stu- dents (20%) were more likely than traditional students (13%) to be undecided about a practice location. More CD students in 7-year programs, more CD students in private schools, and more female CD students were uncertain about practice location than were CD stu- dents in 6- or 8-year programs, in public schools, or male CD students—6-year students = 14%, 7-year stu- dents = 26%, 8-year students = 23%, %2(12, N=479) = 29.3, p = .004; students in private schools = 28%, students in public schools = 15%,X2(6,/V=479) = 19.3, p = .004; females = 24%, males = 15%, %2(6, N = 473) = 17.2,p = .009. Twenty-two percent of the premedical students were undecided about practice location. Fewer CD students (8%) than traditional students (18%) planned to practice in socioeconomically de- prived areas. Even fewer premedical students (2%) indicated such plans. Similarly, fewer CD and premed- ical students saw access to medical care as a problem than did traditional students (Table 4). However, CD students (64%) were more likely than traditional stu- dents (56%) to be uncertain about plans to provide service to socioeconomically deprived areas. CD stu- dents in 7-year programs were more prone to indecision in this regard than were CD students in 6-year pro- grams—6-year students = 60%, 7-year students = 71%, 8-year students = 65%, x2(4, N = 478) = 12.4, p = .01. Again, more female CD students were undecided about these plans than were their male counterparts—females = 68%, males = 61%, %2(2, W = 472) = 12.6, p = .002. Forty-three percent of the premedical students were undecided about this prospect. In contrast to traditional students, CD students were less likely to agree that physicians had an ethical duty to treat infectious patients despite risks to themselves (Table 4). No associations were obtained between this perception on the one hand and program characteris- tics, gender, ethnicity, and occupations of fathers of CD students on the other hand. But premedical students agreed with CD students on this issue (Table 4). Discussion On entry to their respective schools, both CD and traditional students expressed a strong orientation for service to others. Both were highly motivated by the biomedical aspects of medicine and attracted by the types of colleagues they expected to find in medicine. Although they had definitely chosen medicine as a career goal, they typically were uncertain about the specific career paths they would follow in medicine in the future. At the same time, the profile of the CD and tradi- tional students' perspectives on becoming a physician differed in several respects. CD students chose medi- cine as a career goal earlier in life than did their tradi- tional counterparts. CD students can be considered "early deciders."4 CD students were more prone to emphasize factors such as status, income, and job secu- rity in deciding to become physicians than were tradi- tional students. On the other hand, CD students were less likely than traditional students to agree that physicians' income, prestige, and independence will be impaired in the future, and they were less concerned about the potential interference of medicine with family life or other interests. In these ways, compared to traditional students, CD students perceived medicine more positively. Slightly more CD students than tradi- tional students were interested in entering clinical prac- tice. Last, CD students tended to be less sensitive than traditional students to issues surrounding the un- derserved and patients with contagious diseases. How can these differences be explained? Among the program characteristics examined, the public or private control of the school in which a CD program was offered was rarely associated with the differences in the perspectives of CD and traditional students. On the other hand, curricular length of the CD programs was associated with when CD students decided definitely to enter medicine, partly with why they chose medicine, with a perceived disadvantage to the practice of medi- cine, with preferred career activities, and with indeci- sion regarding practice location. Additional studies of students in CD programs should explicate the mecha- nisms underlying these and other potential differences between students in 6-, 7-, and 8-year CD programs. 106 Downloaded by [University of California Santa Barbara] at 06:10 27 June 2016

STUDENTS IN COMBINED DEGREE PROGRAMS Among the background characteristics examined, gender and Asian heritage of CD students were associ- ated with several differences between the CD students' and traditional students' perspectives on becoming a physician. More specifically, the gender of CD students emerged as a significant correlate of indecision sur- rounding specific career plans. This relation is consis- tent with other research on gender and career decisions.5 The Asian background of CD students was also related to several reasons for choosing medicine as a career, notably with the importance of the encourage- ment of other people in the CD students' decision to become a physician. This latter association may de- serve special attention because premedical students rated the encouragement of others as much less import- ant in their decision to study medicine than did CD students. Thus, it may be the Asian heritage of CD students, not age, that accounts for the difference in the importance they and traditional students gave to others in their career choice. . Nevertheless, of all the background characteristics examined, the age differential between CD and tradi- tional students may offer the most promising explana- tion for their different perspectives on becoming physicians. Why? First, CD and premedical students were similar in many respects. They tended to select medicine as a definite career goal at an early age; they agreed on why they wanted to be physicians; they viewed many of the potential disadvantages of medi- cine similarly; and they typically concurred on career plans and beliefs involving the underserved and pa- tients with contagious diseases. Second, the ethnic backgrounds and occupations of fathers of both pre- medical and traditional students were relatively similar, whereas premedical and CD students were relatively dissimilar in these respects. Together, these results prompt the conjecture that at least some of the differ- ences in the perspectives of CD and traditional students reflect relatively limited life experiences. A more sys- tematic study of premedical, CD, and traditional stu- dents would illuminate this speculation. The possibility of helping to shape students' perspec- tives on medicine has been identified as an important rationale for CD programs.6 That rationale would be reinforced if the differences between CD and tradi- tional students' perspectives obtained in this study are indeed due to an age effect. More particularly, CD programs would be well positioned to enable students to maintain their early optimism and to foster in them an empathic and well- informed responsiveness to pressing health care problems. Further, CD students' more positive orientation toward medicine, combined with enhanced program flexibility7 and diminished pressure,8'9 might ultimately increase the number of physicians who address health care issues construc- tively. In times when student attitudes toward medicine may contribute to fewer medical school applica- tions,1011 the more favorable views of CD students take on added significance. Last, several findings of this collaborative study validate the pilot study conducted at Brown Univer- sity.2 As in the earlier study, CD students were more likely to be female, have an Asian background, and have physician parents. CD students at Brown Univer- sity held similar positive orientations toward medicine, as did their peers in this collaborative study, and were largely undecided regarding career plans as well. In these ways, the innovative approach of combined-de- gree programs to medical education may well recruit students different from those entering more traditional pathways to the MD degree. Conclusions CD and traditional students differed in some of their background characteristics, perceptions of medicine, and career plans. Future work using a longitudinal study design should study these differences further. The relation between premedical and traditional students should also be investigated more systematically. Fol- low-up studies need to be conducted to ascertain whether CD students maintain their early optimism toward medicine. References 1. Maheux B, Béland F, Pineault R, Rivest P, Valois L.
